title: What is EV/EBITDA?
subtitle: The most common multiple in M&A and business comparisons
openingQuestion: Why is EV/EBITDA better than P/E when comparing businesses with different capital structures?
openingOptions: P/E cannot be applied to these companies at all
EV/EBITDA is neutral to debt and to depreciation
EV is always lower than Market Cap for any company
EV/EBITDA is simply easier to calculate by hand
explanation: EV/EBITDA compares total enterprise value - market cap plus debt minus cash - against profit before interest, tax, and depreciation. Because both the numerator and denominator sit above both creditors and shareholders, this metric isn't skewed by capital structure the way P/E is, which is why it's the default multiple in mergers and acquisitions. One limitation to remember: EBITDA ignores capital spending, so it inflates the apparent cash-generating power of capital-intensive industries.

Because it ignores capital structure, two differently-leveraged companies can be compared

realWorldExample.description: In telecom M&A deals, EV/EBITDA is the most commonly used valuation metric because it allows a fair comparison between target companies with very different capital structures (debt ratios for infrastructure investment).

quiz.question: Why is EV/EBITDA usually higher for the tech industry than for retail?
options: Tech companies' Enterprise Value is lower, so the multiple rises
Tech companies use more fixed capital than retail
Retail almost never generates a stable positive EBITDA
The market expects higher growth and margin expansion
quiz.explanation: A high-growth business with margins that can expand → the market pays a premium (high EV/EBITDA). Retail grows slowly with thin margins → lower EV/EBITDA. Growth expectations are what gets priced into the multiple.

quiz.question: Why do investment bankers in M&A deals almost always prefer EV/EBITDA over P/E to value a target company?
options: Because the buyer also takes on existing debt, so an all-in price is needed
Because P/E cannot legally be applied to any unlisted target company in a deal
Because EV/EBITDA usually produces a lower valuation than P/E
Because EBITDA is audited while net profit is not
quiz.explanation: In an M&A deal, the buyer acquires the entire business, including its existing debt obligations - EV correctly reflects this 'all-in package' price, while P/E only looks at it from the shareholder's perspective (Equity Value), ignoring the debt the buyer also has to carry.

quiz.question: Market cap is 800 billion, debt is 300 billion, cash is 100 billion, EBITDA is 200 billion. What is the EV/EBITDA?
options: 4.0x (EV = 800; forgetting debt and cash)
6.0x (EV = 800 + 300 + 100; mistakenly adding cash)
5.5x (EV = 800 + 300 − 100 + 100; counting cash twice)
quiz.explanation: EV = Market Cap + Debt − Cash = 800 + 300 − 100 = 1,000 billion. EV/EBITDA = 1,000/200 = 5.0x. Cash is subtracted because the buyer could use that very cash to offset part of the purchase price.

quiz.question: Two companies have identical EBITDA, but one borrows far more than the other. Which metric is correct for comparing them?
options: P/B, since book value doesn't depend on debt
P/E, since it already reflects real interest expense
EV/EBITDA, since this metric is neutral to capital structure
Net profit margin, since it normalizes by revenue
quiz.explanation: The more heavily-indebted company pays more interest, has lower Net Income, and looks like it has a higher P/E - despite having an identical core business. EV/EBITDA sits above both debt and equity, so it's unaffected by how a business raises capital.

quiz.question: What weakness of EBITDA should users of EV/EBITDA keep in mind?
options: It changes with capital structure exactly like net profit does
It's affected by differing tax rates between countries
It can only be calculated for a business with large fixed assets
It ignores the capital spending needed to sustain operations
quiz.explanation: EBITDA adds depreciation back, so a business that constantly must replace equipment looks identical to one that needs no investment at all. This is why EBITDA has been called profit before everything bad.

keyTakeaways: EV/EBITDA is neutral to capital structure and depreciation
The most common multiple in M&A
High-growth industries have a higher EV/EBITDA

practicePrompt.question: Company A borrows heavily (large interest expense, large depreciation from debt-funded assets), Company B carries almost no debt. Why do M&A analysts usually prefer EV/EBITDA over P/E when comparing two companies with such different capital structures?
options: Because EV/EBITDA is neutral to capital structure: EBITDA is calculated before interest and depreciation
Because EV/EBITDA always gives the exact same result as P/E, so it doesn't matter which one you use
Because EV/EBITDA only applies to a debt-free company, and can't be used to compare a highly leveraged one
Because P/E is more accurate than EV/EBITDA in every case when comparing companies
practicePrompt.explanation: EV/EBITDA is neutral to capital structure and depreciation because EBITDA is calculated before subtracting interest, tax, and depreciation - removing the difference caused by how a company finances itself (borrowing heavily or not). This is why EV/EBITDA is widely preferred for M&A valuation and cross-industry/cross-capital-structure comparisons.

application.title: Calculate EV/EBITDA
application.message: Estimate a company's Enterprise Value (market cap + debt − cash), then divide by EBITDA, and compare against the same company's P/E to see how far apart the two metrics land.
application.secondary: EV/EBITDA is useful when comparing companies with different capital structures.

sections.text: EV/EBITDA is the most common valuation multiple in M&A and cross-capital-structure business comparisons - because it looks at the whole enterprise level, before accounting for debt and tax.

sections.label: The formula
sections.text: EV/EBITDA = Enterprise Value / EBITDA  (EV = Market Capitalization + Debt − Cash)
Why EV/EBITDA is fairer than P/E across different capital structures

Two companies with identical EBITDA but different debt levels will have noticeably different Net Income (and P/E) - the more heavily-indebted company pays more interest, has lower Net Income, and looks like it has a higher P/E even though its core business is equivalent. EV/EBITDA completely removes this effect because it's calculated at the EBITDA level (before interest, tax, depreciation) and uses Enterprise Value (which already adds back debt) as the numerator - those two companies will have a much closer EV/EBITDA, better reflecting the true value of their operations.
Why investment banks prefer EV/EBITDA in M&A

In an M&A deal, the buyer isn't just buying shareholders' equity - they're taking on the entire business, including its existing debt obligations. EV/EBITDA correctly reflects this 'all-in' price the buyer actually has to pay, while P/E only looks at it from the shareholder's perspective (Equity Value), ignoring the debt the buyer still has to carry. This is why in telecom M&A deals - where target companies have very different capital structures (infrastructure debt ratios) - EV/EBITDA is almost always the preferred metric.

items: EV/EBITDA is neutral to capital structure (debt/equity) and different depreciation policies between companies
High-growth industries with expanding margins (tech): EV/EBITDA is usually higher as the market pays a premium for growth
Slow-growth industries with stable margins (traditional retail): EV/EBITDA is usually lower
EV/EBITDA can be used even when a company's Net Income is negative, as long as EBITDA is still positive - an advantage P/E doesn't have

lines: When comparing two companies with substantially different capital structures, EV/EBITDA is almost always the fairer choice over P/E.

sections.title: Putting numbers into the formula
sections.equation: EV = Market cap + Debt − Cash · EV/EBITDA = EV ÷ EBITDA

example.title: Two companies, same EBITDA, different capital structures
example.calculation: A: market cap VND 800bn, debt 400bn, cash 100bn → EV 1,100bn · B: market cap 1,000bn, no debt, cash 100bn → EV 900bn · both EBITDA 100bn
example.explanation: B looks dearer on market cap (1,000 against 800) but is in fact cheaper: 9x against 11x. A's VND 400bn of debt is something the buyer takes on, so it belongs in the price paid. P/E cannot see this, because it looks only at the equity.
